findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher never checks the grant type (wrong offsets and inverted condition)
findings.body:
The grant shortcut sits at characters 4–5 of the prefix (e.g. `onrtac`), but `items[0].substring(3, 5)` takes characters 3–4. For `onrtac` that yields `ta`.

The condition is also inverted: it returns `false` when the extracted value equals the expected shortcut.

The two bugs cancel out. `substring(3,5)` never equals a real grant shortcut, so the early return never fires and the matcher only checks that the suffix is a UUID. `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` therefore pass for any grant shortcut, including `na`.

If only the offsets were fixed, every correct token would fail. A prefix shorter than 5 characters also throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of a clean mismatch.

Fix: `return items[0].length() == 6 && items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut) && isUUID().matches(items[1]);`

findings.title: rawTokenId null check validates grantType instead
findings.body:
The fourth check is `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`. It re-checks `grantType`, so a null `rawTokenId` is never rejected.

An `AccessTokenContext` with a null raw ID can be built. `encodeTokenId` would then silently produce an ID like `onrtac:null` instead of failing fast. It should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

findings.title: New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom grant type factories and can block server startup
findings.body:
`getShortcut()` is added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` as an abstract method with no default. The OAuth2GrantType SPI exists so that custom grants can be deployed.

Custom factories compiled against the previous SPI will fail when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `gtf.getShortcut()` on every registered grant factory. They will throw `AbstractMethodError` during server startup, preventing Keycloak from booting.

A custom factory that returns `null` causes a `NullPointerException` from `ConcurrentHashMap.put` in the same `postInit`.

Provide a default implementation (or a fallback when the shortcut is missing or invalid). Encoding should degrade to the unknown grant (`na`) instead of failing startup or token issuance.

findings.title: Javadoc says shortcut is ~3 letters, but the encoding requires exactly 2 characters and nothing validates it
findings.body:
The javadoc tells implementers the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters". `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId` requires the encoded prefix to be exactly 6 characters, 2 per field, and throws `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise.

Neither `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` nor the lazy refresh in `getShortcutByGrantType` validates shortcut length. A custom grant that follows the documentation will issue access tokens whose IDs cannot be decoded. Any later consumer of `getTokenContextFromTokenId` (introspection, userinfo, token exchange, as planned) would then fail for those tokens.

Fix the javadoc to require exactly 2 characters and validate length (and non-null) when registering shortcuts.

findings.title: Client credentials (and other flows) never set the GRANT_TYPE attribute, so their tokens encode grant as 'na'
findings.body:
The grant type is only put into the `ClientSessionContext` in these places:
- `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse`
- ROPC
- refresh
- PreAuthorizedCode
- `StandardTokenExchangeProvider`

`ClientCredentialsGrantType` builds its response with `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` directly and does not call `createTokenResponse`. Its access tokens are therefore encoded as `...na:<uuid>` rather than `...cc:<uuid>`, even though the `cc` shortcut is registered here. The unit test's `trltcc` example implies `cc` is expected.

The same applies to UMA/permission grant tokens (`pg`) and the legacy V1 token-exchange providers. This undermines the stated purpose of letting endpoints rely on the encoded grant type.

Set `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` in these code paths too.

findings.title: testIncorrectGrantType passes because of a NullPointerException, not the intended validation
findings.body:
The factory is built without `postInit`, so `sessionFactory` is null. When `ac` is not found in `grantsByShortcuts`, `getGrantTypeByShortcut` falls into the refresh branch and calls `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws `NullPointerException`.

The test catches any `RuntimeException`, so it passes without ever reaching the `IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value ... for grant type")` path it is meant to verify.

Catch `IllegalArgumentException` specifically, and stub or mock the session factory so the unknown-shortcut path is actually exercised.

findings.title: Public Context copy constructor removed from SPI class
findings.body:
`public Context(Context context)` was deleted from `OAuth2GrantType.Context`. This change is unrelated to the feature. Any extension that wraps or copies the grant context (e.g. custom grant types delegating to another grant) will no longer compile or link.

If removal is intended, it should be called out as a breaking change. Otherwise keep the constructor and copy the new `grantType` field in it.

findings.title: grantType derived once in constructor and not updated by setFormParams
findings.body:
`grantType` is computed from `formParams` only in the constructor. `setFormParams(...)` replaces `formParams` but leaves `grantType` unchanged.

Any caller that swaps the form parameters gets a `getGrantType()` value that no longer matches them. That stale value is what `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse` and ROPC write into the client session context and encode into the token ID.

Either update `grantType` in `setFormParams` or derive it lazily from the current `formParams`.

findings.title: Lazy refresh can silently overwrite an existing shortcut mapping
findings.body:
The duplicate-shortcut validation runs only in `postInit`. When a grant type is hot-deployed later, `getShortcutByGrantType` (and `getGrantTypeByShortcut`) does `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` without checking whether that shortcut already belongs to another grant.

A colliding shortcut replaces the existing mapping. Tokens previously issued for the original grant would then decode to the wrong grant type.

Use `putIfAbsent` and reject or log the conflict, applying the same uniqueness check as in `postInit`.
